jeffery.metin: xliii, 71; lvi, 18; lxxvi, 15; lxxxviii, 14. A goblet. It occurs only in early Sūras in descriptions of the pleasures of Paradise, and was recognized by some of the early authorities as a Nabataean word (cf. as-Suyūtˢī, Itq, 319; Mutaw, 60).1 Some, of course, endeavoured to derived it from , but this verb is obviously denominative (TA, i, 464; LA, ii, 225). The word is commonly used in the early poetry, cf. ʚAdī b. Zaid, al-Aʚshā (Geyer, Zwei Gedichte, i, 56 = Dīwān, ii, 21), ʚAbda b. atˢ-Tˢabīb,2 etc., and seems to have been an early loan-word from Aram., as Horovitz, Paradies, 11, has noted, though Aram. ; Syr. ! both seem to be from the Byzantine κοῦπα (Lat. cupa, cf. Fraenkel, Vocab, 25), from the older Gk. κύμβη.3 %
